Async SQLAlchemy through a D1 driver is not (see `d1`). ## Sources - https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/languages/python/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/languages/python/packages/fastapi/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/ - https://pyodide.org/en/stable/usage/packages-in-pyodide.html - https://blog.cloudflare.com/python-workers-ga === cloudflare/containers # Cloudflare Containers: reaching them and what they cost verified: 2026-10-04 Answers how an existing container image runs on Cloudflare, how traffic and bindings reach it, its sizes and sleep behaviour, and what it costs. Distilled from documentation while weighing a move of a Python API image onto Cloudflare; nothing was run. ## Knowledge - Containers have been GA since 2026-04-13 and need Workers Paid. Any Linux image runs, so native libraries and gRPC clients work. - A container is reached only through a Durable Object, with `getContainer(env.X, id)` or `ctx.container` inside the object, so every request to it goes through a Worker and a Durable Object. - Bindings (D1, R2, KV, Durable Objects) do not reach the container directly. Its outbound HTTP goes through outbound handlers, programmable egress proxies mapped per host with `outboundByHost`. Code inside the container reaches D1 through its REST API or a Worker acting as a proxy, and R2 through its S3 API. - Instance types run from lite (1/16 vCPU, 256 MiB, 2 GB disk) through basic (1/4, 1 GiB, 4 GB), standard-1 (1/2, 4 GiB, 8 GB), standard-2 (1, 6 GiB, 12 GB) and standard-3 (2, 8 GiB, 16 GB) to standard-4 (4, 12 GiB, 20 GB). The image cannot exceed the instance disk. Each account has 50 GB of image storage. - Cold starts are "often 1-3 s". The container sleeps after `sleepAfter`, 10 min by default. Disk is ephemeral and resets on each start. Shutdown sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL up to 15 min later. - Pricing is per 10 ms of active running. Workers Paid includes 25 GiB-hours of memory, 375 vCPU-minutes and 200 GB-hours of disk a month; beyond that $0.0000025 per GiB-second, $0.000020 per active vCPU-second and $0.00000007 per GB-second of disk. Egress is $0.025/GB in North America and Europe with 1 TB included. An always-on 1 GiB instance comes to about $7 a month; one that sleeps most of the time fits inside the included hours. ## Sources - https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/platform-details/limits/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/platform-details/outbound-traffic/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/pricing/ === cloudflare/d1 # D1: SQLite on Cloudflare, migrations and drivers verified: 2026-10-04 Answers what D1 offers as a database, how it is reached, how its schema is migrated, and whether SQLAlchemy and Alembic can drive it. Distilled from documentation and package inspection while weighing a Postgres-to-D1 move; nothing was run against D1. ## Knowledge - D1 runs on SQLite's engine with the JSON extension, FTS5 and math functions. `PRAGMA foreign_keys` and `defer_foreign_keys` are available. `run()` returns `meta.changes`, so a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE status = ...` can be checked by its row count. `batch()` runs its statements as one transaction. - Limits on Paid: 10 GB per database (500 MB on Free), 2 MB per row or value, 100 bound parameters per query, 1,000 queries per Worker invocation. Each database is single-threaded. - Pricing on Paid includes 25 billion rows read, 50 million rows written and 5 GB a month; beyond that $0.001 per million reads, $1.00 per million writes and $0.75 per GB-month. No egress charges. - From a Worker it is a binding. From anything else, such as a container, the only documented route is the REST API. - Migrations are hand-written `.sql` files in a `migrations/` folder, created with `wrangler d1 migrations create`, applied with `--local` or `--remote`, and tracked in a `d1_migrations` table. There is no down migration: a failing migration rolls back itself and the earlier ones stay. Time Travel keeps 30 days of point-in-time restore on Paid (7 on Free). - Read replication is GA at no cost; without the Sessions API every query goes to the primary, and with it reads are sequentially consistent. - `sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1` (0.4.1, 2026-10-02) connects over the REST API or a Python Worker binding. Its async engine is unavailable inside Workers, its `commit` and `rollback` are no-ops because every statement auto-commits, and its package contains no Alembic support. No other package connects Alembic to D1; Alembic's offline `--sql` output written into D1's migration files is an untested route. ## Sources - https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/pricing/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/limits/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/reference/migrations/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/reference/time-travel/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/best-practices/read-replication/ - https://pypi.org/project/sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1/ === cloudflare/r2 # R2: S3 access, presigned URLs and pricing verified: 2026-10-04 Answers whether code written for an S3-compatible bucket works against R2, how presigned URLs behave, and what R2 costs. Distilled from documentation while weighing a move of an audio bucket onto R2; nothing was run. ## Knowledge - boto3 works against the S3 API with `endpoint_url=https://.r2.cloudflarestorage.com` and `region_name="auto"`. - Presigned URLs support GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE, expire from 1 second to 7 days, and work only on the `*.r2.cloudflarestorage.com` host, not on a custom domain. A service that answers with a redirect to a presigned GET keeps working with new credentials and endpoint. - A custom domain gives caching and access control through Access or WAF token authentication. `r2.dev` is rate-limited and meant for development only. From a Worker, an R2 binding is also available. - Standard storage is $0.015 per GB-month with 10 GB-month free; Class A operations $4.50 per million with 1 million free a month, Class B $0.36 per million with 10 million free. Egress is free. Infrequent Access is $0.01 per GB-month, with higher operation prices, a $0.01/GB retrieval fee and a 30-day minimum. ## Sources - https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/buckets/public-buckets/ === cloudflare/vitest-plugin # Testing Workers and Workflows with the vitest plugin verified: 2026-10-04 Answers how Cloudflare's vitest integration tests Workflows and outbound HTTP, and what replaced its removed fetch mock. Distilled from the plugin's type declarations, changelog and examples, and the docs; nothing was run. ## Knowledge - `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` is the renamed `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` (renamed in 1.0.0; the old name stopped at 0.22.0). Tests run inside workerd with the project's wrangler bindings. - Workflow introspection is documented and supported. `introspectWorkflowInstance(binding, id)` gives `waitForStepResult`, `waitForStatus`, the output and error, and `modify(fn)` with `disableSleeps`, `mockStepResult`, `mockStepError`, `forceStepTimeout` and `mockEvent`. `introspectWorkflow(binding)` applies the same `modify` to every instance created afterwards, for ids the test does not control. Both support `await using`. - `modify` works on whole steps. A mocked step never runs its callback, so the HTTP calls inside it never happen; steps that are not mocked run their real code, `fetch` included. `modify` needs a Workflow binding. A Workflow taken from `ctx.exports` raises an error that explains how to add the binding. - `fetchMock` from `cloudflare:test` was removed in 0.13.0 and the `miniflare.fetchMock` option in 0.20.0. The changelog points to mocking `globalThis.fetch` or MSW ("recommended"), and the examples include an MSW fixture set up through `setupFiles`. The prose docs mention neither. - Miniflare's `outboundService` replaces a Worker's whole outbound traffic with a handler; whether the plugin accepts it as an option is unstated. - Whether MSW or a patched `globalThis.fetch` catches a `fetch` made inside a Workflow step is undocumented. The Workflow engine runs in a Durable Object, and the examples only cover requests made from the Worker itself. - Code-level seams, such as a global symbol the code reads for a test double, are not a documented Workflow-testing method; they put the test hook in production code paths. ## Sources - https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/testing/vitest-integration/test-apis/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/test-workflows/ - https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk (vitest-plugin CHANGELOG, `fixtures/vitest-plugin-examples/request-mocking`, `fixtures/vitest-plugin-examples/workflows`) === cloudflare/cf-cli # The cf CLI against wrangler verified: 2026-10-04 Answers what Cloudflare's new `cf` CLI is, how it relates to wrangler, and whether it covers D1 migrations, deploys and CI yet. Distilled from the package, its README, the announcement and the help output; the subcommands' flags were not readable. ## Knowledge - `cf` (npm `cf`, binaries `cf` and `cloudflare`) is in open beta since 2026-09-28; another Cloudflare post calls it a technical preview. Releases ship almost daily. - Cloudflare presents it as wrangler's eventual replacement: when the beta ends, wrangler gets a final major release pointing to `cf`, then 18 months of maintenance. `cf migrate` converts a wrangler project, and configuration moves to a typed `cloudflare.config.ts`. - `cf d1 migrations` and `cf d1 time-travel` exist, but their file format and flags were not documented. `cf deploy` covers Workers and Containers rollouts. - It builds with Vite by default and hands builds to wrangler for projects that need it, Python Workers among them; it documents no Python flow of its own. - Locally it runs against Miniflare with D1, R2 and KV state. In CI it reads `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`; there is no official GitHub Action yet. - wrangler stays GA. Its D1 migrations are hand-written `.sql` files tracked in `d1_migrations`, Python Workers deploy through `pywrangler`, and CI uses `cloudflare/wrangler-action` v4. ## Sources - https://github.com/cloudflare/cf - https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-cf-cli-launch/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/reference/migrations/ - https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/wrangler/commands/d1/ === modal/web-endpoints # Calling a Modal function without the Python client verified: 2026-10-04 Answers how code that cannot run Modal's Python client, such as a Worker or any non-Python service, starts a Modal function and collects its result. Distilled from Modal's documentation; nothing was run. ## Knowledge - Modal's Python client talks gRPC, so it only runs where CPython and grpcio do. Modal has no public REST API to spawn a function and poll a call by id. - The documented route is a web endpoint the app defines itself (`@modal.fastapi_endpoint`, `@modal.asgi_app` and similar), protected with proxy auth tokens sent as key and secret headers. - The job-queue pattern uses two endpoints: `POST /submit` calls `fn.spawn.aio(data)` and returns `{"call_id": call.object_id}`; `GET /result/{call_id}` calls `modal.FunctionCall.from_id(call_id).get.aio(timeout=0)` and answers 202 while the call runs and 404 on `OutputExpiredError`. Results expire after 7 days. - The caller then needs only plain HTTP. Whatever the function returns, such as base64-encoded audio, comes back in that JSON body. ## Sources - https://modal.com/docs/guide/webhooks - https://modal.com/docs/guide/job-queue

## 1. New skill: `skills/architecture-exploration/SKILL.md`

```markdown
---
name: architecture-exploration
description: Draws a system's architecture on a canvas and explores ways to change it with the user. It lays the options out side by side, draws a part they share step by step, and redraws the whole chosen option after each decision the user makes, until one architecture remains. The user edits the same canvas. Use when the user wants to see an architecture or compare options for changing one before a design is settled. For a settled design drawn as one page, use mahou:one-page-design.
argument-hint: <the system or the change to draw>
---

Load mahou:basics first, then mahou:canvas. Then read `.mahou/architecture-exploration.md` if present.

# Architecture exploration

The document goes in `canvas/` in the change's scratch folder and is named after what it draws. Every drawing of one exploration shares one document: the system as it stands in a square of its own, then the options and the drawings that follow them.

## Input

Draw what the conversation has established about the system: what the scouts and researchers found, and the decisions the user has settled. When drawing shows a gap, such as a part whose place nobody has stated, ask the user about it.

## A drawing

Draw with the shapes, labels and layout mahou:canvas sets. On top of those:

- **A part is named as the system names it**, with what it runs on and the deployable it belongs to, such as `API: <runtime>` or `<workflow name> (<deployable>/)`.
- **One area per platform or deployable**, labelled with its name. A drawing is one square: an `area` titled after what it shows, such as `<letter>. <option>` or `Chosen: <option>`.
- **A note for what the arrows cannot show**, such as where deferred work runs or what an option gives up, with its arrow to the part it is about.
- **Every shape id starts with the drawing's key**, `<key>-<part>`. A whole drawing can then be moved, spread or copied by its prefix, and its arrows follow through their bindings.

## Exploring

Follow `references/exploration.md`.

## Export

Export through mahou:canvas. Save the SVG next to the document, under the same name.

## What this skill is not

It does not pick an option. The options and every change to them come from the user. It does not commit.
```

## 2. New reference: `skills/architecture-exploration/references/exploration.md`

```markdown
# Exploring options

Each step adds drawings; none removes one the user has not asked to remove.

1. **Lay the options out as a grid.** When a change varies along independent dimensions, such as where the code runs and how deferred work runs, draw one square per combination: one dimension along the rows, the other along the columns, each square titled `<letter>. <value> + <value>`. Keep the same parts in the same places across the squares, so only what differs between them moves. Give each square a note on what that combination implies that its arrows do not show.

2. **The user narrows the grid.** A dropped option stays on the canvas unless the user asks to remove it. When the user changes one value of a dimension, apply the change to every square that has that value. For example, a separate consumer asked for in one queue option goes into every queue square.

3. **Draw a shared part step by step.** When several options share a part whose inside matters, such as a workflow or a pipeline, draw it once in its own square below the grid. Title it with the options it belongs to, and draw each step numbered with the stores and services it reaches.

4. **Draw the chosen option whole.** In a new square, draw the option the user picks with the shared part drawn inline and the neighbouring subsystems it touches, so one drawing shows the whole system.

5. **Redraw after each decision.** When a decision changes the chosen option, draw it again in a new square beside the earlier one, titled `Chosen: <option>`, and keep the earlier one. Leave out what the user has not asked to show yet, such as a fallback. Update the note of every drawing a decision changes.

The exploration ends when the user says which drawing is the architecture.
```

> - **Leave room under a title.** The first shape inside an area sits clear of the area's label.
> - **Nothing overlaps.** No shape, label or arrow sits on another. When a straight arrow would cross a shape or another arrow's label, curve it with `bend` or move its label with `labelPosition`. When labels crowd each other, move the shapes apart.

Answers whether a Python web app, such as a FastAPI service, can run as a Cloudflare Python Worker, which packages it can use, and the limits that bind it. Distilled from documentation and the Pyodide package list while weighing a move of a Python API onto Cloudflare; nothing was run.

## Knowledge

- FastAPI runs through a built-in ASGI connector (`workers.asgi`). ASGI and WSGI support landed 2026-09-02, and Python 3.14 on Pyodide 314.x is the default for compatibility dates from 2026-09-08. Whether an older compatibility date still pins an older Python is undocumented.
- Cloudflare's own pages disagree on the status. A GA announcement is dated 2026-09-21, while a docs page still says beta behind the `python_workers` flag, with `pywrangler` for setup and deploys.
- Packages are pure-Python wheels, PyEmscripten wheels and what Pyodide bundles. Pyodide 314.0.7 ships Pillow, httpx, SQLAlchemy, pydantic, aiohttp, asyncpg and cffi. It does not ship cairosvg (which needs native libcairo), grpcio, boto3, botocore, greenlet, markdown-it-py or google-genai; a pure wheel may still install, but nothing confirms it.
- Nothing built on gRPC runs, so a Python client that talks gRPC, such as Modal's, cannot run there. Pyodide routes HTTP clients through JS `fetch`.
- Limits are the Workers ones: 128 MB memory per isolate including WASM, a 64 MiB uncompressed bundle (changed 2026-09-04), CPU 30 s by default and up to 5 min on Paid, `waitUntil` up to 30 s after the response, 15 min of wall time for queue consumers and cron triggers.
- Cold start uses a memory snapshot taken at deploy; one third-party measurement put it near 1 s.
- Bindings to D1, R2, KV, Durable Objects, Queues, Workflows, Workers AI and service bindings are available from Python. Async SQLAlchemy through a D1 driver is not (see `d1`).

# Cloudflare Containers: reaching them and what they cost

verified: 2026-10-04

Answers how an existing container image runs on Cloudflare, how traffic and bindings reach it, its sizes and sleep behaviour, and what it costs. Distilled from documentation while weighing a move of a Python API image onto Cloudflare; nothing was run.

## Knowledge

- Containers have been GA since 2026-04-13 and need Workers Paid. Any Linux image runs, so native libraries and gRPC clients work.
- A container is reached only through a Durable Object, with `getContainer(env.X, id)` or `ctx.container` inside the object, so every request to it goes through a Worker and a Durable Object.
- Bindings (D1, R2, KV, Durable Objects) do not reach the container directly. Its outbound HTTP goes through outbound handlers, programmable egress proxies mapped per host with `outboundByHost`. Code inside the container reaches D1 through its REST API or a Worker acting as a proxy, and R2 through its S3 API.
- Instance types run from lite (1/16 vCPU, 256 MiB, 2 GB disk) through basic (1/4, 1 GiB, 4 GB), standard-1 (1/2, 4 GiB, 8 GB), standard-2 (1, 6 GiB, 12 GB) and standard-3 (2, 8 GiB, 16 GB) to standard-4 (4, 12 GiB, 20 GB). The image cannot exceed the instance disk. Each account has 50 GB of image storage.
- Cold starts are "often 1-3 s". The container sleeps after `sleepAfter`, 10 min by default. Disk is ephemeral and resets on each start. Shutdown sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL up to 15 min later.
- Pricing is per 10 ms of active running. Workers Paid includes 25 GiB-hours of memory, 375 vCPU-minutes and 200 GB-hours of disk a month; beyond that $0.0000025 per GiB-second, $0.000020 per active vCPU-second and $0.00000007 per GB-second of disk. Egress is $0.025/GB in North America and Europe with 1 TB included. An always-on 1 GiB instance comes to about $7 a month; one that sleeps most of the time fits inside the included hours.

## Sources

# D1: SQLite on Cloudflare, migrations and drivers

verified: 2026-10-04

Answers what D1 offers as a database, how it is reached, how its schema is migrated, and whether SQLAlchemy and Alembic can drive it. Distilled from documentation and package inspection while weighing a Postgres-to-D1 move; nothing was run against D1.

## Knowledge

- D1 runs on SQLite's engine with the JSON extension, FTS5 and math functions. `PRAGMA foreign_keys` and `defer_foreign_keys` are available. `run()` returns `meta.changes`, so a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE status = ...` can be checked by its row count. `batch()` runs its statements as one transaction.
- Limits on Paid: 10 GB per database (500 MB on Free), 2 MB per row or value, 100 bound parameters per query, 1,000 queries per Worker invocation. Each database is single-threaded.
- Pricing on Paid includes 25 billion rows read, 50 million rows written and 5 GB a month; beyond that $0.001 per million reads, $1.00 per million writes and $0.75 per GB-month. No egress charges.
- From a Worker it is a binding. From anything else, such as a container, the only documented route is the REST API.
- Migrations are hand-written `.sql` files in a `migrations/` folder, created with `wrangler d1 migrations create`, applied with `--local` or `--remote`, and tracked in a `d1_migrations` table. There is no down migration: a failing migration rolls back itself and the earlier ones stay. Time Travel keeps 30 days of point-in-time restore on Paid (7 on Free).
- Read replication is GA at no cost; without the Sessions API every query goes to the primary, and with it reads are sequentially consistent.
- `sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1` (0.4.1, 2026-10-02) connects over the REST API or a Python Worker binding. Its async engine is unavailable inside Workers, its `commit` and `rollback` are no-ops because every statement auto-commits, and its package contains no Alembic support. No other package connects Alembic to D1; Alembic's offline `--sql` output written into D1's migration files is an untested route.

# Testing Workers and Workflows with the vitest plugin

verified: 2026-10-04

Answers how Cloudflare's vitest integration tests Workflows and outbound HTTP, and what replaced its removed fetch mock. Distilled from the plugin's type declarations, changelog and examples, and the docs; nothing was run.

## Knowledge

- `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` is the renamed `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` (renamed in 1.0.0; the old name stopped at 0.22.0). Tests run inside workerd with the project's wrangler bindings.
- Workflow introspection is documented and supported. `introspectWorkflowInstance(binding, id)` gives `waitForStepResult`, `waitForStatus`, the output and error, and `modify(fn)` with `disableSleeps`, `mockStepResult`, `mockStepError`, `forceStepTimeout` and `mockEvent`. `introspectWorkflow(binding)` applies the same `modify` to every instance created afterwards, for ids the test does not control. Both support `await using`.
- `modify` works on whole steps. A mocked step never runs its callback, so the HTTP calls inside it never happen; steps that are not mocked run their real code, `fetch` included. `modify` needs a Workflow binding. A Workflow taken from `ctx.exports` raises an error that explains how to add the binding.
- `fetchMock` from `cloudflare:test` was removed in 0.13.0 and the `miniflare.fetchMock` option in 0.20.0. The changelog points to mocking `globalThis.fetch` or MSW ("recommended"), and the examples include an MSW fixture set up through `setupFiles`. The prose docs mention neither.
- Miniflare's `outboundService` replaces a Worker's whole outbound traffic with a handler; whether the plugin accepts it as an option is unstated.
- Whether MSW or a patched `globalThis.fetch` catches a `fetch` made inside a Workflow step is undocumented. The Workflow engine runs in a Durable Object, and the examples only cover requests made from the Worker itself.
- Code-level seams, such as a global symbol the code reads for a test double, are not a documented Workflow-testing method; they put the test hook in production code paths.

## Sources

- https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk (vitest-plugin CHANGELOG, `fixtures/vitest-plugin-examples/request-mocking`, `fixtures/vitest-plugin-examples/workflows`)

# Calling a Modal function without the Python client

verified: 2026-10-04

Answers how code that cannot run Modal's Python client, such as a Worker or any non-Python service, starts a Modal function and collects its result. Distilled from Modal's documentation; nothing was run.

## Knowledge

- Modal's Python client talks gRPC, so it only runs where CPython and grpcio do. Modal has no public REST API to spawn a function and poll a call by id.
- The documented route is a web endpoint the app defines itself (`@modal.fastapi_endpoint`, `@modal.asgi_app` and similar), protected with proxy auth tokens sent as key and secret headers.
- The job-queue pattern uses two endpoints: `POST /submit` calls `fn.spawn.aio(data)` and returns `{"call_id": call.object_id}`; `GET /result/{call_id}` calls `modal.FunctionCall.from_id(call_id).get.aio(timeout=0)` and answers 202 while the call runs and 404 on `OutputExpiredError`. Results expire after 7 days.
- The caller then needs only plain HTTP. Whatever the function returns, such as base64-encoded audio, comes back in that JSON body.

## Sources

- https://modal.com/docs/guide/webhooks
- https://modal.com/docs/guide/job-queue

description: Draws a system's architecture on a canvas and explores ways to change it with the user. It lays the options out side by side, draws a part they share step by step, and redraws the whole chosen option after each decision the user makes, until one architecture remains. The user edits the same canvas. Use when the user wants to see which parts a system has and how they connect, or to compare options for changing them before a design is settled. For a settled design drawn as one page, use mahou:one-page-design.
argument-hint: <the system or the change to draw>
---

Load mahou:basics first, then mahou:canvas. Then read `.mahou/architecture-exploration.md` if present.

# Architecture exploration

The document goes in `canvas/` in the change's scratch folder and is named after the system or the change it draws. Every drawing of one exploration shares one document: the system as it stands in a square of its own, then the options and the drawings that follow them.

## Input

Draw only the parts and connections the conversation has established: what the scouts and researchers found, and the decisions the user has settled. When you reach a part whose place nobody has stated, ask the user where it goes.

## A drawing

Draw with the shapes, labels and layout mahou:canvas sets. On top of those:

- **Name each part with the name the code and the docs use**, followed by its runtime and its deployable, such as `API: <runtime>` or `<workflow name> (<deployable>/)`.
- **Draw one area per platform or deployable**, labelled with its name. Put each drawing in an `area` of its own, titled with the option it draws, such as `<letter>. <option>` or `Chosen: <option>`.
- **Add a note for each fact the diagram leaves out**, such as where deferred work runs or what an option gives up, with an arrow to the part it is about.
- **Start every shape id with the drawing's key**, `<key>-<part>`. To move, spread or copy a whole drawing, select its shapes by the prefix; tldraw keeps their arrows attached through the bindings.

## Exploring

When the user asks how the system could change, or wants options compared, follow `references/exploration.md`. A drawing of the system as it stands needs only the sections above.

## Export

Export through mahou:canvas. Save the SVG next to the document, under the same name.

## What this skill is not

It does not pick an option. The options and every change to them come from the user. It does not commit.

input.content:
# Exploring options

Each step adds drawings. Remove a drawing only when the user asks.

1. **Lay the options out as a grid.** When a change varies along independent dimensions, such as where the code runs and how deferred work runs, draw one square per combination: one dimension along the rows, the other along the columns, each square titled `<letter>. <value> + <value>`. Keep the same parts in the same places across the squares, so only the parts that differ move. Give each square a note on a consequence of that combination the diagram leaves out, such as a client library that cannot run on that runtime.

2. **The user narrows the grid.** A dropped option stays on the canvas unless the user asks to remove it. When the user changes one value of a dimension, apply the change to every square that has that value. For example, when the user asks for a separate consumer in one queue option, add it to every queue square.

3. **Draw a shared part step by step.** When several options share a part made of steps, such as a workflow or a pipeline, draw it once in its own square below the grid. Title it with the options it belongs to, and number each step, with the stores and services it reaches on the same row.

4. **Draw the chosen option whole.** In a new square, draw the option the user picks with the shared part drawn inline and the neighbouring subsystems it touches, so the user sees the whole system in one drawing.

5. **Redraw after each decision.** When a decision changes the chosen option, draw it again in a new square beside the earlier one, titled `Chosen: <option>`, and keep the earlier one. Leave out parts the user has not asked to see yet, such as a fallback. Update the note of every drawing the decision changes.

The exploration ends when the user says which drawing is the architecture.

content.text:
I've fixed all five phrases and the related ones the test turned up, and the verification round found no fix undone. The new rules caught all five phrases from a run over the drafts with no hint of which ones you meant. Only the rewrite for "A part is named as the system names it" needed my own wording. Nothing is written to the plugins yet.

## 1. `skills/architecture-exploration/SKILL.md` (revised)

```markdown
---
name: architecture-exploration
description: Draws a system's architecture on a canvas and explores ways to change it with the user. It lays the options out side by side, draws a part they share step by step, and redraws the whole chosen option after each decision the user makes, until one architecture remains. The user edits the same canvas. Use when the user wants to see which parts a system has and how they connect, or to compare options for changing them before a design is settled. For a settled design drawn as one page, use mahou:one-page-design.
argument-hint: <the system or the change to draw>
---

Load mahou:basics first, then mahou:canvas. Then read `.mahou/architecture-exploration.md` if present.

# Architecture exploration

The document goes in `canvas/` in the change's scratch folder and is named after the system or the change it draws. Every drawing of one exploration shares one document: the system as it stands in a square of its own, then the options and the drawings that follow them.

## Input

Draw only the parts and connections the conversation has established: what the scouts and researchers found, and the decisions the user has settled. When you reach a part whose place nobody has stated, ask the user where it goes.

## A drawing

Draw with the shapes, labels and layout mahou:canvas sets. On top of those:

- **Name each part with the name the code and the docs use**, followed by its runtime and its deployable, such as `API: <runtime>` or `<workflow name> (<deployable>/)`.
- **Draw one area per platform or deployable**, labelled with its name. Put each drawing in an `area` of its own, titled with the option it draws, such as `<letter>. <option>` or `Chosen: <option>`.
- **Add a note for each fact the diagram leaves out**, such as where deferred work runs or what an option gives up, with an arrow to the part it is about.
- **Start every shape id with the drawing's key**, `<key>-<part>`. To move, spread or copy a whole drawing, select its shapes by the prefix; tldraw keeps their arrows attached through the bindings.

## Exploring

When the user asks how the system could change, or wants options compared, follow `references/exploration.md`. A drawing of the system as it stands needs only the sections above.

## Export

Export through mahou:canvas. Save the SVG next to the document, under the same name.

## What this skill is not

It does not pick an option. The options and every change to them come from the user. It does not commit.
```

## 2. `references/exploration.md` (revised)

```markdown
# Exploring options

Each step adds drawings. Remove a drawing only when the user asks.

1. **Lay the options out as a grid.** When a change varies along independent dimensions, such as where the code runs and how deferred work runs, draw one square per combination: one dimension along the rows, the other along the columns, each square titled `<letter>. <value> + <value>`. Keep the same parts in the same places across the squares, so only the parts that differ move. Give each square a note on a consequence of that combination the diagram leaves out, such as a client library that cannot run on that runtime.

2. **The user narrows the grid.** A dropped option stays on the canvas unless the user asks to remove it. When the user changes one value of a dimension, apply the change to every square that has that value. For example, when the user asks for a separate consumer in one queue option, add it to every queue square.

3. **Draw a shared part step by step.** When several options share a part made of steps, such as a workflow or a pipeline, draw it once in its own square below the grid. Title it with the options it belongs to, and number each step, with the stores and services it reaches on the same row.

4. **Draw the chosen option whole.** In a new square, draw the option the user picks with the shared part drawn inline and the neighbouring subsystems it touches, so the user sees the whole system in one drawing.

5. **Redraw after each decision.** When a decision changes the chosen option, draw it again in a new square beside the earlier one, titled `Chosen: <option>`, and keep the earlier one. Leave out parts the user has not asked to see yet, such as a fallback. Update the note of every drawing the decision changes.

The exploration ends when the user says which drawing is the architecture.
```

## 3. `skills/canvas/SKILL.md`: the Drawing bullets (revised; the mockup sentence and the watch change are unchanged)

> - **Draw each kind of part with its own shape.** Draw each of the system's own modules as a rectangle, coloured by the deployable it belongs to. Draw a store as a cylinder, titled with the product that holds the data, such as `<provider> Postgres`, and captioned with the data it holds. Draw an external service as a cloud, the client as an ellipse, and a platform or a deployable as an `area` around its parts.
> - **Label each arrow with the payload or the action it carries**, and with the binding, protocol or credential it goes through when that matters.
> - **Lay a flow out left to right.** Put whoever starts it on the left, stores in a column of their own next to the modules that write them, and external services along the far edge. Draw a process as a vertical column of numbered steps, each with the store or service it reaches on the same row, so its arrow runs straight across.
> - **Leave room under a title.** Keep the first shape inside an area clear of the area's label.
> - **Keep every shape, label and arrow clear of the others.** When a straight arrow would cross a shape or another arrow's label, curve it with `bend` or move its label with `labelPosition`. When labels crowd each other, move the shapes apart.

## 4. Explore, guide and README (revised lines)

- **explore, step 5:** "When the question is **which parts a system has and how they connect**, or how options for changing them compare, load mahou:architecture-exploration …"
- **explore, step 6:** "… such as whether an approach **works** on the real platform …"
- **guide:** "A question about **which parts a system has and how they connect**, or how options for changing them compare, goes to mahou:architecture-exploration, which draws them on a canvas the user edits."
- **README:** "… **It lays the options out** as a grid of small drawings, one per combination, **and draws a part they share step by step.** After each decision it redraws the chosen one whole …"

## 5. Wiki titles

- `python-workers.md`: "Python Workers: what runs and what does not" becomes "**Python Workers: packages, limits and status**".
- `containers.md`: "Cloudflare Containers: reaching them and what they cost" becomes "**Cloudflare Containers: access, sizes and pricing**".

The rest of the wiki drafts are unchanged from last round.

## 6. New: `superpowers/skills/unslop/SKILL.md` (iteration in another plugin)

The existing rules miss these phrases for three reasons:
- **Rule 16 exempts them.** Any bold lead-in that ends in a period and is followed by detail passes, slogans included.
- **Rule 32 doesn't reach them.** It covers code that acts, not a shape or label that "says" or "shows".
- **No rule covers a "what" clause that points at information without giving it.**

I propose three new rules appended under "Plain speech", numbered 39–41 because numbers are stable ids. The first round's prompt copies every rule verbatim, so they apply without any other change.

> 39. **Things that talk.** A shape, label, arrow, name, type, test or drawing that "says", "shows", "tells" or "names" something, used to state a rule or convention. The sentence hides the instruction behind what an artifact communicates, and the reader has to translate it back into what to do. Write the instruction with the reader as the actor: "Shapes say what a thing is" becomes "Draw each module as a rectangle and each store as a cylinder". "A note for what the arrows cannot show" becomes "Add a note for each fact the diagram leaves out, such as where deferred work runs". Rule 32's personified code covers code that acts; this rule covers artifacts that communicate. "The test shows the bug" stays when it reports a real result.
>
> 40. **"What" clauses that withhold the content.** A clause such as "what a thing is", "what flows", "what the arrows cannot show" or "what a system's architecture is" points at information without giving it, and the reader has to guess what belongs there. Replace the clause with the content, or with a concrete example: "label each arrow with what flows" becomes "label each arrow with the payload or action it carries", and "a question about what a system's architecture is" becomes "a question about which parts a system has and how they connect". The clause stays when the words right after it list the content.
>
> 41. **Slogans as bold lead-ins.** A bold lead-in that is a whole claim written as a motto ("**Shapes say what a thing is.**", "**Nothing overlaps.**") rather than a label naming the item. Rule 16's exemption covers a lead-in that names the item; a slogan states the rule indirectly and then the body restates it. Make the lead-in the plain instruction itself: "**Draw each kind of part with its own shape.**"

Approve, correct or drop each item. Once you approve, I write them uncommitted.

- **Playback:** after the Worker's 307 redirect, Chromium plays the audio and seeks, with R2 answering each seek with a partial (206) response.
- **Caveat, the key:** an `<audio>` element can't send the `X-API-Key` header, so the spike passed the key in the URL as `?key=`.
- **Caveat, expiry:** once a presigned URL expires, playback stops with no error shown. The browser never goes back to the Worker for a fresh URL.

The Chromium that was playing audio has closed. `workflow-testing`, `item-workflow` and `local-dev` are still running.

Both rules are quoted below from `superpowers/skills/unslop/SKILL.md`.

**Rule 16**, under Style:
> 16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.

**Rule 32**, under Plain speech:
> 32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.

**Why the phrases got past them**
- **Rule 16** clears a bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item and is followed by new detail. "**Shapes say what a thing is.**" passed as such a lead-in, since the sentences after it add the actual shapes. The rule doesn't separate a lead-in that names the item from one that states the rule as a slogan.
- **Rule 32** already lists aphorisms and personification, so "Shapes say what a thing is" arguably falls under it. But its examples are about code acting ("the plan holds it") and figurative motion verbs ("rides along"). The agent didn't apply it to a shape or label that "says" or "shows".

So proposed rules 39 and 41 partly overlap with 32 and 16. They could instead be written into those two rules: name communication verbs in 32's personification example, and narrow 16's exemption to lead-ins that name the item without making a claim. Rule 40, about "what" clauses, has no existing rule it could join.

Should 39 and 41 stay new rules, or be written into 32 and 16?

# superpowers/skills/unslop/SKILL.md

## Rule 16, extended

Old:
> 16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.

New:
> 16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell. A lead-in written as a slogan, a whole claim stated as a motto ("**Shapes say what a thing is.**", "**Nothing overlaps.**"), does not name the item and falls outside that exemption. Make the lead-in the plain instruction itself: "**Draw each kind of part with its own shape.**"

## Rule 32, extended

Old:
> 32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.

New:
> 32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), artifacts that talk, figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. An artifact talks when a shape, label, arrow, name, type or test "says", "shows" or "tells" something to state a rule: "shapes say what a thing is" becomes "draw each module as a rectangle and each store as a cylinder". A sentence that reports what an artifact really produced ("the test shows the bug") stays. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.

## Rule 39, new, appended after 38

> 39. **"What" clauses that withhold the content.** A clause such as "what a thing is", "what flows", "what the arrows cannot show" or "what a system's architecture is" points at information without giving it, and the reader has to guess what belongs there. Replace the clause with the content, or with a concrete example: "label each arrow with what flows" becomes "label each arrow with the payload or action it carries", and "a question about what a system's architecture is" becomes "a question about which parts a system has and how they connect". The clause stays when the words right after it list the content.

10:## Content
12:1. **Puffery.** "pivotal moment", "testament to", "evolving landscape", "setting the stage for", "indelible mark", "deeply rooted". Cut it and state what happened.
13:2. **Name-dropping.** Listing sources without context. Pick one and say what it said.
14:3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with the actual fact.
15:4. **Promotional language.** "seamless", "robust", "powerful", "groundbreaking", "elegant". Use neutral descriptions.
16:5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "It is widely known", "Some argue". Name the source or delete.
17:6. **Formulaic challenges.** "Despite challenges... continues to thrive." Replace with specific facts.
19:## Language
21:7. **Generated vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant, leverage, utilize, facilitate. Replace with plain words.
22:8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
23:9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly.
24:10. **Rule of three.** Forcing ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
25:11. **Synonym cycling.** The same thing called three names in one paragraph. Pick one and repeat it.
26:12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y are not on a scale. List the items.
28:## Style
30:13. **Em dashes.** Do not use them, and do not replace them with parentheses or en dashes. End the sentence or use a comma.
31:14. **Colons as connectors.** Colons are fine before a list or an example, not as a mid-sentence hinge. Rewrite so the point stands alone.
32:15. **Inline-header lists.** A bold label and colon that restates the line ("**Performance:** Performance improved...") becomes prose. A bold lead-in that names the item and is followed by new detail is fine.
33:16. **Curly quotes.** Replace with straight quotes.
35:## Communication artifacts
37:17. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps", "Let me know if", "Certainly", "Of course". Remove.
38:18. **Cutoff disclaimers.** "While specific details are limited...". Find the fact or remove.
39:19. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question", "You're absolutely right". Remove.
41:## Filler
43:20. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". "It is important to note that" is deleted.
44:21. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly" becomes "may".
45:22. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State a fact or a plan, or end the section.
47:## Jargon
49:23. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate, wedge, vector, locus, nexus, primitive (as noun), harness (as metaphor), surface (as in "API surface"), bedrock, scaffolding (as metaphor), paradigm, north star, flywheel, endgame. Use the concrete word: "base", "add", "way", "the last phase".
51:## Plain speech
53:24. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the data stays close at hand" names a feeling. Name the mechanism or the number instead. If a sentence could appear unchanged in another project's documentation, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
54:25. **Split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop a clause. One idea per sentence.
55:26. **Active voice.** Name the actor: "the compiler validates queries", not "queries are validated". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or does not matter.
56:27. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number. "significantly improves" becomes the measured difference.
57:28. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" becomes "use", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if".
58:29. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor and flourish standing in for a direct statement: "a dial worth turning", "earns its keep", "moves the needle". Say what you mean with the literal phrase.
59:30. **Describing the text instead of writing it.** The sentence's subject is the text itself or a part of it ("this document", "this skill", "this section", "the list below", "the rules here"). Its verb says what the text is, covers, contains, is for or is about to say. The pattern shows up as an opening that states the text's purpose or scope, as an announcement of what follows ("Two things to consider:", "It is worth mentioning that", "which brings us to"), or as a count of the parts. Delete the sentence and check that every fact is still in the text. If a fact appears only in the deleted sentence, state that fact about the subject instead. "This section explains how the cache expires. Entries expire after an hour." becomes "Cache entries expire after an hour." A heading names the content. It does not count the content or announce it.
60:31. **Saying the same thing twice.** Say each thing once. Cut a sentence that repeats, at the same level of detail, something the text already says. The earlier mention can be anywhere in the text, title and description included. Examples: a closing sentence that recaps the paragraph, an "in other words" that paraphrases, an opening that restates the heading or the description. Keep a repetition only when it adds precision, a concrete example, or a translation of a term that the first mention assumed the reader knew. Also keep a summary that reduces a concept spread over several paragraphs to its main points.
61:32. **Pronoun referent overload.** The same pronoun standing for two different things in one sentence, or a relative pronoun dropped where the wrong attachment is the easier parse. "The counts alone do not show a sentence appearing twice, a unit whose text also appears inside the unit before it, or any text it says was left behind": the first "it" is the unit, the second is the tool from the sentence before, and "any text it says was left behind" dropped its "that", so "it says" reads as the verb until "was" breaks the parse. Name the referent, or restore the "that": "inside the previous unit", "any text the tool says was left behind". 25's backtrack test finds the sentence, but splitting cannot repair it: a short sentence can still make the reader resolve one word twice.
62:33. **Actions turned into nouns.** An event or action written as a noun phrase ("the server failing to start", "the removal of the file", "validation of the input") and then made the subject of a weak verb ("goes in the chat", "happens", "takes place", "is needed"). The reader has to unpack the noun back into who does what to what. Write the clause with its actor and its verb: "Only the server failing to start goes in the chat" becomes "When the server fails to start, tell the user in the chat", and "Validation of the input happens in the parser" becomes "The parser validates the input". A noun stays when it names something the text keeps referring to, such as a defined term ("the migration", "the release").
64:## Exclusions

  "- Payloads: params, events and non-stream step results are each capped at 1 MiB. Since 2026-03-26 a JS step can return a `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>`, which the cap does not count. Otherwise larger artifacts go to external storage (R2) with a reference passed instead."),
 ("treat the Agents SDK table as stale.\n",
  """treat the Agents SDK table as stale.
- A Workflow class is written in TypeScript or JavaScript (GA since 2025-04-07) or Python (open beta since 2025-08-22, no later GA entry). Python has the same step API in decorator form (`@step.do`, `step.sleep`, `step.wait_for_event`). Rust cannot define one: workers-rs has no `WorkflowEntrypoint`. Whether stream returns and the CPU setting work from Python is undocumented.
- A step is ordinary Worker code, so it reaches code in other languages through what it can call: a service binding to another Worker, a Container through its Durable Object, or plain HTTP. A Worker in another script starts the Workflow through a binding with `script_name`; whether that works across languages is undocumented.
- Steps per instance: 10,000 by default on Paid, configurable to 25,000 (1,024 on Free); `step.sleep` does not count as a step. State per instance is up to 1 GB on Paid.
- Testing: see `vitest-plugin`.
"""),
 ("- REST instances create/get: https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/resources/workflows/subresources/instances/",
  "- REST instances create/get: https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/resources/workflows/subresources/instances/\n- Python Workflows: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/python/\n- workers-rs Workflows issue: https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-rs/issues/663"),
])

(M / W / 'cloudflare/INDEX.md').write_text("""# Cloudflare

- [`cf-cli`](cf-cli.md): the beta `cf` CLI against wrangler for D1 migrations, deploys and CI
- [`containers`](containers.md): running an existing image behind a Durable Object, reaching bindings, sizes, sleep and cost
- [`d1`](d1.md): SQLite on Cloudflare, its limits, wrangler migrations, and why SQLAlchemy and Alembic do not drive it
- [`durable-objects`](durable-objects.md): serializing work per key with a gate object

The same pronoun standing for two different referents in one sentence ("the unit before it" where "it" is the unit, "any text it says was left behind" where "it" is the tool from the previous sentence) makes the reader hold both candidates and test each against what follows. A dropped relative pronoun does the same: "any text it says was left behind" has lost its "that", so "it says" reads as the verb until "was" breaks the parse. The trap is sharpest when the referent sits in an earlier sentence while a nearer candidate of the same kind sits in this one. Name the referent ("inside the previous unit", "any text the tool says was left behind") or restore the "that". A short sentence can still make the reader resolve one word twice; length is not what makes this readable.
69:Write actions as verbs, not as nouns. An event turned into a noun phrase ("the server failing to start", "the removal of the file", "validation of the input") and hung on a weak verb ("goes in the chat", "happens", "takes place") makes the reader unpack who does what. Write the clause with its actor and its verb: "Only the server failing to start goes in the chat" becomes "When the server fails to start, tell the user in the chat", and "Validation of the input happens in the parser" becomes "The parser validates the input". A noun stays when it names something the text keeps referring to, such as a defined term.

"Which brings us to the next point" just goes. The same applies to headings: name what is in the section ("Issues found", "Considerations"), do not count it or trail it ("Two things to consider", "What follows"). A count also goes stale as soon as an item is added or removed.
64	
65	Do not say the same thing twice. A second pass over an idea, in different words at the same level of detail, gives a reader who understood the first pass nothing. It shows up as a closing sentence that recaps the paragraph above it, an "in other words" that paraphrases instead of sharpening, or a trailing clause that restates the sentence it hangs off. 67	Make every pronoun resolve once, to one thing. Each spike's folder has a `FINDINGS.md`, the combined write-up is `.scratch/cloudflare-migration/spikes/REPORT.md`, and the repo's tracked files are unchanged.

| # | Spike | Result | What matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | image-processing | Works, with caveats | resvg-wasm (SVG to PNG) and @jsquash/webp ran in a deployed Worker and in a Workflow step, at 25–530 ms of CPU per image. They add 1.5 MiB gzipped to the Worker. The raster output matches Pillow byte for byte. Images above about 10 MP run out of memory, and the code can't catch it. Text in an SVG disappears unless a font is bundled. Cloudflare's Images binding rejects every SVG, but it handles a 36 MP raster. |
| 2 | modal-http | Works | A step fetched the audio from Modal and wrote it straight into R2 (1.95 MB here, 12.2 MB in `item-workflow`). Both the `X-Api-Key` header and Modal's proxy auth work. **This contradicts the docs:** a step that returned 2.6 MB also succeeded, though the documented limit is 1 MiB. |
| 3 | item-workflow | Works, with caveats | A 70-minute article used 39 steps, so the default 10,000 steps covers about 13.8 h of audio. Retries are per step, and a failed instance can restart from a given step. Taking the domain's lease works two ways: the queue sends the waiting item an event, or the item polls the queue. **A deploy fails every step that's running at that moment and runs it again.** Sometimes the failure only registers at the step's timeout, and the item holds its domain's lease until then (15 min observed). |
| 4 | cross-script-binding | Works | The API deploys without the pipeline and answers `workflow.not_found`. It starts working within seconds of the pipeline deploying. Sleeping instances resume on the new code after a redeploy. |
| 5 | shared-d1 | Works, with caveats | The conditional claim had exactly one winner in 45 of 45 races across the two Workers. A failing migration rolls back completely. Two migration runs at the same time race, and the loser exits with an error. JSON columns come back as strings. Applying migrations with a limited-permission API token, as CI would, wasn't tried. |
| 6 | r2-presigned | Works, with caveats | Only tested in Chromium. `<audio>` can't send the key header, so the spike passed the key in the URL. An expired URL stops playback with no error. |
| 7 | firecrawl-gemini | Works, with caveats | **Firecrawl's SDK fails inside a Worker; plain HTTP requests work.** Gemini through AI Gateway works. The existing cassettes match only if the matcher rewrites the URL and compares bodies as JSON. The spike's calls appear in the `nagara` gateway's logs. |
| 8 | local-dev | Works | Already reported. |
| 9 | workflow-testing | All approaches work, with caveats | MSW does catch requests made inside a step. Only intercepting HTTP, through MSW or miniflare's `outboundService`, runs the real step code and replays cassettes. Only introspection skips sleeps and retry delays. A mocked step result that's falsy is ignored, and the real step runs. Requests that match nothing reach the real network unless `outboundService` catches them. |

**Cleanup**
- **Deleted:** 4 Workflows, 10 `nagara-spike-*` Workers with their secrets and Durable Object namespaces, 2 D1 databases, and 3 R2 buckets after deleting their 43 objects.
- **Checked by listing again:**
  - Workers: only `nagara` remains. Workflows: only `extraction`.

- **Images:** what happens to images above 10 MP: drop them, shrink them through the Images binding, or send only those to it? Which fonts ship for SVG text?
- **TTS:** does the Worker stream the audio into R2, or does Modal write it there directly? `X-Api-Key` or Modal's proxy auth? How is the "start synthesis" call kept from starting twice when a deploy re-runs it?
- **Lease:** event or polling? Is it released after the recipe step or at the end of the item? What timeout do steps holding it get, and when do deploys happen?

- **D1:** which deployable owns the migrations, and what stops two CI runs from applying them at once? Where does the shared `Item` type live?

# General Coding Style Guide

* Use conventional commits

* Avoid creating intermediate variables when possible; only case it might make sense is when the intermediate variable makes the code easier to understand and follow
* Do not write obvious, narrative comments (e.g. explaining what a variable holds or restating what the next line does). Good naming and types already convey the *what*. Only add a comment when it explains the **WHY** behind a non-obvious decision (a hidden constraint, a workaround, a subtle invariant), or to disambiguate a confusing **block** of code whose intent isn't clear from reading it. If removing the comment wouldn't leave a future reader confused, don't write it.

# TypeScript Coding Style Guide

- When checking for a null or undefined value in any language, use the explicit syntax `value == null`.
- When creating new types, use existing types as base if available (e.g. extending interfaces or referencing their properties).
- Never use TypeScript's enum, instead use a constant map and derive the type from it.
- By default, assume each function or component must be defined in its own module, unless specified otherwise or it has high cohesion with another element and it might make sense to keep them together.

# React Coding Style Guide

## General

- Always use named exports.
- Prefer assigning arrow functions to a variable over using a function declaration.
- When trying to install node dependencies, check the available lock file on the root folder to determine which tool to use.

## Imports and Component Structure

- Always import React internals (e.g. `useState`, `useEffect`) by name from the React module, never use the default import.
- Colocate related code (state, effects, functions) within a component to improve readability. Place common code above the blocks where it is used.
- Each function or component should be defined in its own module by default, unless it has high cohesion with another element.

## Component Definition

- Always use arrow functions for React components; do not use the `React.FC` type.
- Destructure props directly in the function arguments when defining a component.
- When generating a component's props interface, always use the `Props` name.

## JSX and Rendering

- Within JSX, always use ternary operators for conditional rendering.
- Avoid nested ternaries in JSX.
- Use Panda-css syntax for styling: `className={css({ color: "red" })}`.
- Always add a comma after the last item in an object or array.

## React Query

- Unless the project is following a different pattern, always aim to use react-query for remote data fetching and manipulation
- Avoid destructuring queries and mutations.

# Python Coding Style Guide

- **Dependency management**: I use poetry for dependency management, so make sure to use it to
    install dependencies and run commands.
- **Explicit Null Checks**: When checking for a null value, always use explicit syntax: `value is None`.
- **Optional Types**: Use the newer `| None` syntax for optional types instead of `Optional[]`.
- **Type Hints**: Use type hints throughout your code for clarity and type safety.
- **Testing**: Write tests for all new code, using pytest and relevant fixtures.

# Writing style
Mannered prose substitutes metaphor and flourish for direct statement. Instead of "a parameter worth varying," the mannered writer produces "a dial worth turning." Instead of "this point still matters," they write "this point earns its keep." The phrases exist to display the writer, not to convey the idea, and readers can tell. That is why mannered prose irritates: it makes the reader work harder so the writer can perform. It is also imprecise. Metaphors drag in connotations the writer did not choose and cannot control.
Never ever use mannered prose or metaphors on your writing, always say what you mean directly, no need to embellish or use complicated prose to impress the reader.

Do not describe the message inside the message. Some of your words refer to the subject you are writing about; others refer to the text itself, to how many parts it has, what order they come in, that something is about to arrive, or that you are about to say it. That second kind tells the reader nothing, because the thing being announced arrives in the very next words anyway. Delete it, then check that every fact survived the deletion.

These spans hide anywhere in a sentence, not only in front of a colon. "Two things to take into account:" and "One thing worth doing now:" and "Processing X, the next step is:" sit at the front. "The config is fine, but there is one thing worth flagging here" buries it mid-sentence. "I should mention that the build fails on ARM" becomes "the build fails on ARM". "Which brings us to the next point" just goes. The same applies to headings: name what is in the section ("Issues found", "Considerations"), do not count it or trail it ("Two things to consider", "What follows"). A count also goes stale as soon as an item is added or removed.

Do not say the same thing twice. A second pass over an idea, in different words at the same level of detail, gives a reader who understood the first pass nothing. It shows up as a closing sentence that recaps the paragraph above it, an "in other words" that paraphrases instead of sharpening, or a trailing clause that restates the sentence it hangs off. Before writing one, ask what the reader can do or know after the second version that they could not after the first. If the answer is nothing, cut it. Keep the restatement only when it adds precision, gives a concrete example, or translates a term the first version assumed the reader knew.

Make every pronoun resolve once, to one thing. The same pronoun standing for two different referents in one sentence ("the unit before it" where "it" is the unit, "any text it says was left behind" where "it" is the tool from the previous sentence) makes the reader hold both candidates and test each against what follows. A dropped relative pronoun does the same: "any text it says was left behind" has lost its "that", so "it says" reads as the verb until "was" breaks the parse. The trap is sharpest when the referent sits in an earlier sentence while a nearer candidate of the same kind sits in this one. Name the referent ("inside the previous unit", "any text the tool says was left behind") or restore the "that". A short sentence can still make the reader resolve one word twice; length is not what makes this readable.

Write actions as verbs, not as nouns. An event turned into a noun phrase ("the server failing to start", "the removal of the file", "validation of the input") and hung on a weak verb ("goes in the chat", "happens", "takes place") makes the reader unpack who does what. Write the clause with its actor and its verb: "Only the server failing to start goes in the chat" becomes "When the server fails to start, tell the user in the chat", and "Validation of the input happens in the parser" becomes "The parser validates the input". A noun stays when it names something the text keeps referring to, such as a defined term.

Give the content, not a pointer to it. A clause like "what a thing is", "what flows" or "what the arrows cannot show" points at information without giving it, and the reader has to guess what belongs there; write the information or a concrete example instead ("label each arrow with the payload or action it carries"). An artifact that talks does the same: a shape, label or test that "says" or "shows" something is a rule hidden behind the artifact, so write the rule as an instruction ("draw each module as a rectangle"). A bold lead-in is a label naming the item or the instruction itself, never a slogan such as "**Shapes say what a thing is.**"

# Other notes

## Executing root restricted actions

If you ever need to execute a root restricted action (e.g. using `sudo` to call a CLI tool), you can use `pkexec` to provide the user a way to give your action the adequate permissions to run.
