`restart()` resolves as soon as Cloudflare accepts the restart, before any step runs. I ran 10 restarts through the cross-script binding, 5 with `restart({ from: { name: "b" } })` and 5 with `restart()`. The promise resolved in 382–627 ms (median 387 ms), and `status()` read right after resolution returned `queued` every time. Step `b`'s start row reached D1 3.1–3.8 s after resolution (median 3.4 s) in both variants, and never before it. `status()` stayed `queued` for about 3 s and showed `running` only around the time the step started. `restart()` with no arguments ran step `a` again, starting it 2.9–3.5 s after resolution; restarting from `b` did not. A retry route that relies on the step to write "generating" leaves the D1 row in its failed state for about 3.5 s after `restart()` returns.

The "b start" column comes from the timestamp step `b` wrote, which is on the pipeline Worker's clock. The "Seen" column is when the API Worker's own polling found that row, measured on the same clock as the resolve time. "Seen" was 100–460 ms later in every run, so the difference between the two clocks is small.

| Run | Variant | Resolve (ms) | b start − resolve (ms) | Seen − resolve (ms) | `status()` after resolve | `a` ran again |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| f1 | from `b` | 384 | 3565 | 3738 | queued | no |
| f2 | from `b` | 627 | 3205 | 3448 | queued | no |
| f3 | from `b` | 407 | 3320 | 3570 | queued | no |
| f4 | from `b` | 383 | 3834 | 4293 | queued | no |
| f5 | from `b` | 525 | 3302 | 3401 | queued | no |
| n1 | none | 534 | 3450 | 3653 | queued | yes (+3258) |
| n2 | none | 388 | 3545 | 3776 | queued | yes (+3353) |
| n3 | none | 382 | 3407 | 3546 | queued | yes (+3190) |
| n4 | none | 387 | 3147 | 3392 | queued | yes (+2950) |
| n5 | none | 386 | 3683 | 4085 | queued | yes (+3521) |

All ten instances ended `complete`. Restarting from `b` waited about as long as restarting from the beginning, so the gap comes from Cloudflare scheduling the instance, not from replaying steps that already ran.

Running `wrangler delete` on the Workflow's Worker left the Workflow in place; it needed a separate `wrangler workflows delete`.

Branches 4 and 5 are approved. Branch 6, Image handling, is now open on the canvas, with the decisions explore, shape and the spikes already made about images:

- **Rasters:** every raster goes through the Images binding, and no image library runs inside the Worker.
- **SVGs:** an SVG stays an SVG, with its scripts stripped before it's stored.
- **Dropped images:** rasters under 200 px are dropped, and so is any image that fails to fetch or process, recorded as a degradation.
- **Storage:** each image is stored once per content hash, with its content type on the object.
- **Describing:** Gemini, through AI Gateway with its response cache on, describes a raster from the image and an SVG from its markup sent as plain text. A failed describe falls back to the alt text.
- **Costs:** every describe writes a ledger row at the flat price, marked cached when the gateway's cache answered.

Correct anything that's wrong with a sticky note. The open questions come next.

3:summary: "The Gemini describer: one generated sentence for a block a listener can't see, reused by the code path and the image path, floored and capped against one shared per-item budget."
12:Gives a listener one spoken sentence for a block they cannot see: a code block, or an image with no author-written text. It is a reusable core with two callers: the code path and the image path both reach the same Gemini call, layered under a fan-out that floors, caps, and fails per unit. It never speaks what a block *means*, only what it *is* or *shows*: meaning comes from the author, and the describer only makes the block visible. Implemented in `api/app/service/describe.py`, called during enrichment (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)).
25:| `ImageDescribeRequest` | one image the precedence flagged for a describe (case 2): its `index` in the unit list, its raw `alt`, and the WebP `image` bytes |
79:`enrich_with_descriptions` walks the interleaved unit list once into one document-ordered job list of every code unit and every flagged image. That single ordered list is what makes the cap a shared budget across both kinds.
83:    J["jobs in document order: code units + flagged images"] --> C{"within the per-item cap?"}
84:    C -->|beyond cap| Floor["code floors; image keeps its precedence fallback; degrade: cap reached"]
85:    C -->|within cap| G["asyncio.gather(return_exceptions=True), under a semaphore"]
89:    W --> S{"code units within cap and none resolved?"}
95:**One shared budget, counted in document order.** `NAGARA_DESCRIBE_MAX_PER_ITEM` (default 25) caps the combined code-and-image total, so the two kinds can never each spend a full budget. Past the cap a code unit floors and an image keeps its precedence fallback; each records a `describe cap reached` degradation. The cap never fails an item and never goes silent.
110:**Per-unit failure degrades, systemic failure fails the item.** A single unit failing writes a `describe failed` degradation and floors (code) or keeps the fallback (image). The item fails only when there are code units within the cap and **every one** of them failed: a code-bearing item with zero code descriptions is a silent total failure, an outage rather than an article state. An image-only failure never raises, because an image always has a spoken fallback.
115:Each successful call fires an `on_describe(kind)` callback, which the lifecycle meters as one `describer` cost entry per call; a failed or capped unit made no billable call, so only the success branch counts.
119:- **No describer cache.** Per-row resume already covers the common retry case. What is lost is cross-article dedup of the same snippet, second-order on cost; a cache does not defend against abuse, and the retry count cap and quota enforcement, which is not built yet, own that instead.
docs/technical-design/article-extraction.md:94:Validation runs on the **decoded bytes**, never on HTTP or HTML metadata. The bytes are sniffed for an `<svg` root; a raster image is opened with Pillow and **kept when `min(width, height) >= 200`**, measured on the decoded file. What survives is re-encoded to WebP keyed by its content hash (see [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md) for the storage seam this shares) and the hash becomes the unit's image reference, so no origin URL leaks into persisted markdown.

I read the describer and article-extraction notes and added the rules that stay as they are today to branch 6:
- **Code blocks:** the describe step covers code blocks as well as images.

- **Failed describes:** a failed describe floors a code block or leaves an image on its fallback. The item fails only when every code block within the budget failed.
- **Rasters:** kept rasters are re-encoded to WebP, now through the Images binding.

With those added, branch 6 has no open questions. Confirm the leaves, or correct any rule that should change in the migration, and I'll draw the write-up.
